title: Class 13: Grassroots Environmental Movements in India

slides.title: Introduction to Indian Environmental Movements
slides.continuity_bridge: Environmental protection in India did not start in government offices or international summits; it began in remote villages where everyday survival depended on trees, clean water, and fertile soil.
slides.eli15_takeaway: In India, environmental movements are not weekend hobbies for rich nature-lovers. They are fierce survival battles by poor villagers defending the water, firewood, and soil they need to stay alive.
key_facts: Lecture date: October 26, 2026.
Core conflict: Grassroots community survival versus state-sponsored commercial exploitation.
Key distinction: Indian movements focus on human livelihood security and basic rights, unlike Western recreation-focused wilderness preservation.
Direct dependence: Rural and tribal populations rely on open forests and rivers for daily fuel, livestock fodder, and food.
slides.mental_model: Western conservation is like visiting an art museum on Saturday; Indian grassroots ecology is like physically blocking thieves from raiding your kitchen pantry.

checkpoint.question: What fundamentally distinguishes Indian grassroots environmental movements from early Western conservationism?
options: Indian movements fight for direct survival and local livelihoods, while Western movements focused on preserving scenic wilderness for recreation
Indian movements rely exclusively on corporate funding
Indian movements aim to industrialize protected forests
Indian movements reject non-violent protests
checkpoint.explanation: Indian grassroots movements fight for basic survival and livelihood resources (water, fodder, soil), differing sharply from Western preservation driven by recreation.

slides.title: The Bishnoi Faith & Ecological Ethics
slides.continuity_bridge: To see how deep these survival roots go, we trace India's green struggles back to 15th-century Rajasthan, where a spiritual community made protecting nature an unbending way of life.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Over 500 years ago in Rajasthan's harsh desert, Guru Jambheshwar founded the Bishnoi faith on 29 strict rules, ordering his followers to protect green trees and wild animals with their own lives.
key_facts: Founder: Guru Jambheshwar (Jambhoji), born 1451 in Western Rajasthan.
Name origin: 'Bishnoi' means 29 ('Bish' = 20, 'Noi' = 9), representing 29 core spiritual and ecological commandments.
Strict ecological bans: Total prohibition on felling green trees and hunting wild animals or birds.
Sacred species: The Khejri tree (Prosopis cineraria), blackbucks, chinkaras, and peafowl.
Desert ecosystem role: Khejri fixes soil nitrogen, yields nutrient-rich fodder (sangri), and survives severe droughts.
slides.mental_model: Treating a desert tree like an oxygen tank inside a spaceship: puncture the tank or cut the tree, and the entire crew suffocates in the wasteland.

checkpoint.question: What core ecological rule did Guru Jambheshwar mandate for the Bishnoi community?
options: Never cut down green trees and show compassion to all living animals
Clear scrub forests to expand camel grazing
Sell desert timber to urban lime kilns
Hunt blackbucks once a year during festivals
checkpoint.explanation: Guru Jambheshwar's 29 commandments strictly forbid felling green trees—especially the drought-resistant Khejri tree—and mandate total sanctuary for wild animals.

slides.title: Khejarli Massacre (1730) & Living Legacy
slides.continuity_bridge: Guru Jambheshwar's ecological rules were not empty words; in 1730, they faced their ultimate real-world test when the King of Jodhpur sent axemen to clear a sacred desert grove.
slides.eli15_takeaway: In 1730, Amrita Devi and 362 Bishnoi villagers let royal soldiers chop off their heads with axes rather than allow their sacred Khejri trees to be cut down.
key_facts: Event & Date: September 1730 at Khejarli village near Jodhpur, Rajasthan.
Perpetrator: Royal soldiers sent by Maharaja Abhai Singh of Jodhpur to fell wood to burn lime for a new royal palace.

Immortal declaration: Amrita Devi Bishnoi hugged a Khejri tree and declared: 'Sir santhe rookh rahe to bhi sasto jaan' (If a tree is saved even at the cost of one's head, consider it a cheap bargain).
Death toll: 363 Bishnoi men, women, and children were decapitated while shielding trees.
Royal outcome: Maharaja Abhai Singh halted all logging, apologized in person, and issued a royal copper-plate decree permanently banning tree-felling and hunting in Bishnoi lands.
Modern vigilance: The community continues active anti-poaching patrols, leading to the landmark 1998 prosecution in the Salman Khan blackbuck hunting case.
slides.mental_model: Human shields in a bank robbery, except instead of protecting bags of paper cash, villagers stepped in front of battle-axes to save trees that shielded them from desert famine.

checkpoint.question: What historic bargain did Amrita Devi Bishnoi proclaim before her execution in 1730?
options: If a tree is saved at the cost of one's head, consider it a cheap bargain
Fell the trees if the king pays gold to the village
Take our livestock instead of our timber
Trees belong to the state and not to God
checkpoint.explanation: Amrita Devi famously proclaimed 'Sir santhe rookh rahe to bhi sasto jaan', asserting that trading human life to save a tree that feeds the whole ecosystem is a worthy bargain.

slides.title: Chipko Movement: Seeds of Resistance in Gopeshwar
slides.act: Act 2: Forest Huggers of the Mountains & Ghats
slides.continuity_bridge: Two hundred and forty years after the Khejarli massacre, the fight against commercial axemen flared up again—this time on the steep, landslide-prone slopes of the Garhwal Himalayas.
slides.eli15_takeaway: When forest officers denied poor hill farmers 10 ash trees to carve wooden plows, but handed those same forests to an athletic company to make cricket bats, angry mountain villagers organized to fight back.
key_facts: Geography: Gopeshwar, Chamoli district, Garhwal Himalayas, Uttarakhand (then Uttar Pradesh).

Direct spark (1973): State Forest Department refused local farmers 10 ash trees for plow yokes, yet leased the same forest tract to the Simon Sports Goods company for cricket bats and tennis racquets.
Grassroots base: Dasoli Gram Swarajya Sangh (DGSS), founded in 1964 by Chandi Prasad Bhatt.
DGSS purpose: Built village forest cooperatives to create local jobs and stop rural youth from migrating away in poverty.
slides.mental_model: A city council banning you from taking firewood for your winter stove, then selling the neighborhood park to a luxury factory to make designer ping-pong paddles.

checkpoint.question: What direct injustice sparked the 1973 Chipko protests in Gopeshwar?
options: The forest department banned local farmers from cutting wood for plow yokes while giving ash trees to a commercial sports goods company
Villagers demanded the right to clear forest for commercial paper mills
The state shut down a local iron mine
Foreign companies tried to divert mountain rivers into bottled water plants
checkpoint.explanation: The Forest Department denied mountain peasants a few trees for farm tools, yet leased those exact trees to a commercial sports goods company for cricket bats.

slides.title: Frontline Tactics: Chandi Prasad Bhatt & Gaura Devi
slides.act: Act 2: Forest Huggers of the Mountains & Ghats
slides.continuity_bridge: Faced with armed commercial lumberjacks, Gopeshwar villagers needed a non-violent tactic powerful enough to stop an axe in mid-swing without shedding blood.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Chandi Prasad Bhatt invented the tree-hug tactic, and 50-year-old Gaura Devi led 27 village women to block armed loggers at Reni village when contractors tried to sneak in while the men were away.
key_facts: Tactic genesis: Chandi Prasad Bhatt declared: 'When their men raise their axes, we will embrace the trees to protect them' (Chipko = 'to cling' in Hindi).
Reni village standoff: March 1974 in Reni village, near the Nanda Devi border.
Leader: Gaura Devi, a 50-year-old widow leading the village Mahila Mangal Dal.
The deception: Government officials lured village men to Chamoli town to collect compensation money, leaving the forest unguarded.
Frontline clash: Gaura Devi and 27 village women stood on a narrow mountain ledge, confronting armed loggers: 'The forest nurtures us like a mother; chop us before you chop the trees!'
Outcome: Loggers and contractors dropped their axes and fled without cutting a single trunk.
slides.mental_model: A hockey goalkeeper blocking a puck with their body: women placed their bare bodies between steel axes and tree trunks because clear-cutting the slopes meant mudslides would crush their homes.

checkpoint.question: How did Gaura Devi and the Mahila Mangal Dal stop commercial loggers at Reni village in March 1974?
options: They stood on the trail and hugged the trees, daring loggers to axe human bodies before touching wood
They burned down the logging camp and stole the axes
They filed a legal injunction in the Supreme Court that morning
They offered cash compensation to the sports goods company
checkpoint.explanation: Gaura Devi and 27 local women physically wrapped their bodies around trees when loggers tried to exploit the absence of village men, forcing the contractors to withdraw.

slides.title: Chipko Spreads: Bahuguna, USV & Ecological Economics
slides.act: Act 2: Forest Huggers of the Mountains & Ghats
slides.continuity_bridge: Gaura Devi proved that mountain women could defeat commercial loggers; now, regional leaders had to turn that local spark into national law.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Sunderlal Bahuguna walked 5,000 kilometers across the Himalayas to spread a radical truth: trees are worth far more alive holding mountain soil than dead on a lumber truck.
key_facts: Key leader: Sunderlal Bahuguna completed an epic 5,000 km foot march (padayatra) from Kashmir to Kohima, giving Chipko global visibility.
Iconic philosophy: 'Ecology is permanent economy'—coined by Sunderlal Bahuguna.
Core women leaders: Sarla Behn and Mira Behn (Gandhian disciples from Lakshmi Ashram), Bachni Devi, and Sudesha Devi.
Allied youth wing: Uttarakhand Sangharsh Vahini (USV) mobilized students against forest timber auctions.
Movement folk anthem: 'What do the forests bear? Soil, water, and pure air; Soil, water, and pure air are the basis of life.'
Landmark policy victory: In 1980, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi enacted a 15-year statutory ban on commercial green felling above 1,000 meters elevation in the Himalayas.
slides.mental_model: Mountain trees are like structural steel rebar inside concrete. Pull out the rebar to sell scrap metal, and the entire hillside slides into the valley and drowns the plains in mud.

checkpoint.question: What core ecological slogan did Sunderlal Bahuguna coin during the Chipko movement?
options: Ecology is permanent economy
Dams are modern temples
Timber export brings prosperity
Fell green trees to build fast roads
checkpoint.explanation: Bahuguna argued that living mountain forests provide permanent water and soil stability, generating ecological value that far exceeds one-time timber sales.

slides.title: Chipko in Action: Padayatras & Village Assemblies
slides.act: Act 2: Forest Huggers of the Mountains & Ghats
slides.continuity_bridge: Chipko succeeded not through television or newspapers, but through relentless foot marches and open-air meetings held beneath the forest canopy.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Activists hiked hundreds of miles along steep mountain trails, gathering entire villages under tree canopies to organize non-violent patrols and keep illegal timber merchants away.
key_facts: Mobilization tactic: Padayatras (long-distance foot marches) connecting isolated valleys without motor roads.
Community governance: Mahila Mangal Dals and village elders met in assemblies to schedule patrols and track logging permits.
Strict non-violence: Followed Gandhian satyagraha principles—no physical violence, no weapons, and no personal harm to laborers.
Inter-valley solidarity: Villagers shared rations and blankets across snowy passes to sustain 24/7 vigil points.
slides.mental_model: A neighborhood watch on mountain footpaths: without phones or internet, the whole village gathers under a banyan tree to set up night patrols and guard the slope.

checkpoint.question: Why were foot marches (padayatras) so critical for spreading Chipko across the Himalayas?
options: They enabled direct contact with isolated mountain villages lacking roads or telecommunications to build collective resistance
They were required by state forestry laws to register complaints
They generated ticket revenue to purchase chainsaws
They carried harvested timber down to urban markets
checkpoint.explanation: Padayatras enabled activists to reach isolated Himalayan villages on foot, using folk songs and open assemblies to build a unified, non-violent defense network.

slides.title: Appiko Movement: Karnataka's Southern Forest Huggers
slides.act: Act 2: Forest Huggers of the Mountains & Ghats
slides.continuity_bridge: When the government banned commercial logging in the northern Himalayas, timber contractors shifted their axes south to the tropical rainforests of the Western Ghats.
slides.eli15_takeaway: In 1983, villagers in Karnataka's Western Ghats hugged rainforest trees to stop the state from clear-cutting native jungle to plant commercial teak and eucalyptus monocultures.
key_facts: Location & Date: September 1983 in Salkani village, Sirsi taluk, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka (Western Ghats).
Leader: Pandurang Hegde (inspired by Chipko after training under Sunderlal Bahuguna).
Linguistic meaning: 'Appiko' means 'to hug' in Kannada.
Root cause: State forest department clear-cut diverse tropical rainforests to plant fast-growing commercial teak and eucalyptus monocultures.
The Threefold Mandate (UBV in Kannada): 1. Ubsu (Save existing forest); 2. Belesu (Grow new native trees); 3. Balasu (Use forest resources rationally).
The Five Fs of village survival: Food, Fodder, Fuel, Fiber, and Fertilizer.
Grassroots innovations: Distributed fuel-saving smokeless chulhas (Astra stoves) and built domestic gobar-gas digesters to slash firewood demand.
slides.mental_model: Ripping out a thriving grocery store offering grains, vegetables, and fruit (the 5 Fs) just to fill the shelves with rows of useless plastic poles (monoculture teak).

checkpoint.question: What do the '5 Fs' championed by the Appiko movement in Karnataka stand for?
options: Food, Fodder, Fuel, Fertilizer, and Fiber
Farming, Finance, Fisheries, Freight, and Factories
Flora, Fauna, Feathers, Ferns, and Fungus
Fast, Fierce, Flexible, Focused, and Formal
checkpoint.explanation: The Appiko movement was built on three core mandates in Kannada: Ubsu (Save), Belesu (Grow), and Balasu (Rational Use) to protect Western Ghats biodiversity.

slides.title: Save Silent Valley: Kunthipuzha Dam & The Macaque
slides.continuity_bridge: While forest villagers fought off commercial axes, a far more destructive threat targeted India's rivers: giant hydroelectric dams that could drown entire valleys underwater forever.
slides.eli15_takeaway: In Kerala, scientists and poets united to stop a hydroelectric dam that would have drowned an ancient 50-million-year-old rainforest and wiped out the rare Lion-tailed Macaque.
key_facts: Location: Silent Valley on the Kunthipuzha River, Palakkad district, Western Ghats, Kerala.
Threatened project: In 1970, the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) planned a 120 MW dam submerging 8.3 sq km of undisturbed tropical rainforest.
Ecological indicator: Primatologist Steven Green and Romulus Whitaker (BNHS) proved in 1971–72 that the valley was a crucial sanctuary for the endangered Lion-tailed Macaque (Macaca silenus).
People's science group: Kerala Sasthra Sahithya Parishad (KSSP) published techno-economic studies showing the dam generated trivial power while destroying irreplaceable evolutionary biology.
Public leaders: Poet Sugathakumari, ornithologist Dr. Salim Ali, and Dr. V.S. Vijayan mobilized national opinion.
Court stay: Activist N.V. Krishna won a High Court stay order in August 1979.
Government cancellation: In January 1981, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi canceled the dam; Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi formally inaugurated Silent Valley National Park in 1985.
Historic significance: India's first environmental victory fought strictly to protect non-human biodiversity rather than human resource gathering.
slides.mental_model: Burning down an ancient library containing one-of-a-kind manuscripts written over millions of years, just to boil a single cup of tea.

checkpoint.question: Why was the Save Silent Valley campaign in Kerala unique among Indian environmental struggles?
options: It was fought primarily to protect biodiversity and an endangered monkey species rather than human displacement or timber rights
It was funded by international logging corporations
It was led by state electricity engineers against local farmers
It resulted in building the tallest arch dam in Asia
checkpoint.explanation: Silent Valley was uninhabited by human settlements; the campaign succeeded purely on ecological grounds to protect ancient rainforest genetics and the Lion-tailed Macaque.

slides.title: Kali Bachao Andolan: Fighting Dam Cascades & Paper Mills
slides.continuity_bridge: Silent Valley saved one pristine river, but just north in Karnataka, the Kali River was already choked by six major dams and suffocating under toxic factory slime.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Grassroots activists stopped a 7th mega-dam and fought industrial paper mill poisons in Karnataka's Kali River, but paid a tragic price when lawyer Ajit Nayak was murdered for taking polluters to court.
key_facts: Geography: Kali River flows 184 km through Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, draining into the Arabian Sea.
Dam cascade: 6 large dams (including Supa Dam) had already submerged 32,000 acres of Western Ghats forest; a proposed 7th dam threatened 210 more hectares.
Industrial pollution: West Coast Paper Mills in Dandeli discharged toxic black liquor effluent, while illegal sand mining gouged out riverbanks.
Movement leadership: Pandurang Hegde and the Kali Bachao Andolan spearheaded protests against the 7th dam and paper mill toxicity.
Project cancellation: Dropped after a TERI Environmental Impact Assessment documented unacceptable forest loss and poor economic returns.
Tragic price: On July 27, 2018, 58-year-old environmental lawyer Ajit Nayak was murdered in Dandeli for filing public interest litigation against illegal sand mafias.
slides.mental_model: A patient who has already survived six bypass surgeries being forced into a seventh while breathing toxic smoke—the river reached its absolute biological breaking point.

checkpoint.question: What two grounds led authorities to drop the proposed 7th hydroelectric dam on the Kali River?
options: An environmental assessment showing heavy ecological damage and poor economic returns
A complete drought that dried up the entire river channel
A decision by the state to switch to nuclear energy
Opposition by international tennis companies
checkpoint.explanation: The proposed 7th dam on the Kali River was abandoned after a TERI Environmental Impact Assessment proved the project caused severe forest destruction for minimal electricity gains.

slides.title: Narmada Bachao Andolan: The Battle Over Sardar Sarovar
slides.continuity_bridge: While southern river fights halted individual regional dams, India's largest and most bitter environmental battle erupted across central India along the sacred Narmada River.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Medha Patkar and Baba Amte led hundreds of thousands of indigenous Adivasis against mega-dams on the Narmada River, proving how massive infrastructure often drowns poor farming villages to feed wealthy cities.
key_facts: Geography: 1,312 km Narmada River passing through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat.
Target structures: Sardar Sarovar Dam (Gujarat) and Narmada Sagar Dam (MP).
Project origins: Conceived in the mid-1960s under Jawaharlal Nehru; delayed for decades by interstate water disputes.
Key leaders: Medha Patkar, Baba Amte, and writer Arundhati Roy.
Displacement scale: Over 250,000 predominantly tribal (Adivasi) residents evicted without fair land-for-land resettlement.
Historic turning point (1993): The independent Morse Commission condemned the project, forcing the World Bank to cancel its \$450 million loan—its first loan withdrawal due to environmental protests.
Legal outcome: In 2000, the Supreme Court permitted construction under phased resettlement conditions; the completed dam was inaugurated in 2017.
slides.mental_model: Bulldozing an entire low-income neighborhood to build an expressway, packing residents into temporary plastic tents, while speeding cars drive past.

checkpoint.question: What historic milestone did the Narmada Bachao Andolan achieve in 1993?
options: It forced the World Bank to cancel its loan to the Sardar Sarovar Dam following the independent Morse Commission review
It built the largest solar plant in Asia
It negotiated an outright ban on all dams across India
It converted the Narmada river basin into a wildlife sanctuary
checkpoint.explanation: Relentless protests and documented human rights violations prompted the Morse Commission's scathing report, forcing the World Bank to pull its funding in 1993.

slides.title: Tehri Dam: Himalayan Megastructure & Construction Timeline
slides.continuity_bridge: While Narmada contested the central plains, engineers pushed an even more daring project high in the northern Himalayas: erecting the fifth tallest dam in the world right on the Bhagirathi River.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Tehri Dam is an 855-foot rock-and-earth pyramid built on the Ganga headwaters to generate 2,400 megawatts of power and supply Delhi with drinking water, taking 30 years to build amid relentless protests.
key_facts: Location: Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, on the Bhagirathi River (200 miles northeast of Delhi).
Dimensions: Height of 855 feet (261 meters)—the 5th tallest dam in the world.
Capacity: 2,400 MW hydroelectric output and 300 cusecs of municipal drinking water for Delhi.
Reservoir size: 42 square kilometers, holding 2.6 billion tons of water.

Timeline: Approved in 1972 by UP Irrigation Department; construction halted repeatedly; transferred to Tehri Hydro Development Corporation (THDC) in 1988 with Soviet financing; fully commissioned in 2006.
slides.mental_model: Stacking a 70-story skyscraper of packed rock across a roaring mountain gorge to hold back a lake the size of a city.

checkpoint.question: Where is the Tehri Dam located and what is its primary watercourse?
options: In Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, across the Bhagirathi River
In Palakkad, Kerala, across the Kunthipuzha River
In Sirsi, Karnataka, across the Kali River
In Vadodara, Gujarat, across the Narmada River
checkpoint.explanation: The Tehri Dam is built in the Garhwal Himalayas of Uttarakhand on the Bhagirathi River, one of the primary headstreams of the Ganga.

slides.title: Tehri Dam: Ecological Trauma, Human Rights & TBVSS
slides.continuity_bridge: Tehri's engineering numbers looked heroic on official blueprints, but local communities saw the drowning of their historic valley and the destruction of the holy river.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Tehri Dam devastated the Bhagirathi river ecology, wiped out native fish migration, drowned the historic town of Old Tehri, uprooted 100,000 people, and sparked a 74-day hunger strike by Sunderlal Bahuguna.
key_facts: Ecological disruption: Severe drop in dissolved oxygen, altered water turbidity, and blocked upstream migration for native fish like the Golden Mahseer.
Human displacement: Complete submergence of the historic capital of Old Tehri; over 100,000 residents evicted from fertile valleys.
Corruption scandals: 6 separate inquiries investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) over embezzled rehabilitation funds.
Resistance organization: Tehri Bandh Virodhi Sangharsh Samiti (TBVSS), founded in 1978 by veteran hill activists.
Bahuguna's fast: Sunderlal Bahuguna conducted a 74-day hunger strike at the dam site in 1996 demanding independent reviews.
slides.mental_model: Plugging a living river's throat with concrete: dissolved oxygen collapses, native fish cannot swim upstream to spawn, and the entire biological cycle suffocates.

checkpoint.question: What heroic non-violent protest did Sunderlal Bahuguna undertake against the Tehri Dam in 1996?
options: A 74-day hunger strike on the banks of the Bhagirathi River
A 500-day armed occupation of the powerhouse
A boycott of foreign sports goods companies
An international petition to the United Nations Security Council
checkpoint.explanation: In 1996, Sunderlal Bahuguna staged a 74-day hunger strike at the dam site, forcing the central government to set up an independent review committee.

slides.title: Tehri Dam: Seismic Risk & Broken Government Review
slides.continuity_bridge: Even worse than river pollution and broken relocation promises, seismologists issued a terrifying warning: Tehri Dam was built directly on top of an active Himalayan earthquake fault.
slides.eli15_takeaway: Engineers designed Tehri Dam using 1960s blueprints rated for a magnitude 7.2 earthquake, even though modern geologists warned that a magnitude 8.5 quake could rupture the dam and drown half a million people downstream in hours.
key_facts: Outdated blueprints: Engineering plans finalized in the 1960s before modern plate tectonics and seismic risk modeling were established.
Hazard zone: Sits directly in the seismically active Central Himalayan Seismic Gap, underlain by the Srinagar Fault.
Magnitude gap: Dam engineered for a magnitude 7.2 to 8.4 quake, but geologists (Brune, Gaur) warned of expected earthquakes exceeding magnitude 8.5.
Downstream catastrophe: Structural failure would unleash a wall of water submerging Rishikesh, Haridwar, and settlements housing nearly 500,000 people within hours.
Ignored science: In 1987, a Ministry of Environment expert committee voted unanimously against the dam, but the central government overruled its own scientists.
Broken safeguards: The 1997 Hanumantha Rao Committee recommended vital seismic and rehabilitation safeguards that authorities largely sidelined.
slides.mental_model: Placing a 2.6-billion-ton water tank on rickety wooden stilts in the middle of a bowling alley, betting hundreds of thousands of lives that the ball will never hit the stilts.

checkpoint.question: Why did seismologists and independent expert committees repeatedly urge the cancellation of the Tehri Dam?
options: It was built in the seismically active Central Himalayan fault zone where a magnitude 8.5+ earthquake could trigger a catastrophic dam rupture
The river did not have enough water to spin turbines
The reservoir water was too cold to supply drinking water
The dam was made entirely of wood
checkpoint.explanation: Independent geologists warned that Tehri sits in a dangerous seismic fault gap, where a major earthquake could break the dam and submerge holy cities downstream within hours.

slides.title: Echoes of Resistance: 'A Dam Built with Our Tears'
slides.continuity_bridge: Despite thirty years of scientific warnings, hunger strikes, and courtroom battles, the rising reservoir waters swallowed Old Tehri town, leaving an unforgettable lesson for Indian environmentalism.
slides.eli15_takeaway: As rising reservoir waters swallowed his home and drowned centuries of Himalayan heritage, Sunderlal Bahuguna delivered his mournful final verdict: Tehri is not a monument of progress, but a dam built with our tears.
key_facts: Protest slogan: Hill walls were painted with: 'बाँध नहीं चाहिए, बाँध पहाड़ का विनाश है' ('We do not want the dam; the dam is the mountain's destruction').
Decades of vigil: Sunderlal Bahuguna lived in a modest riverbank hut leading protests from the 1980s until 2004, when reservoir waters finally swallowed his shelter.
Displacement toll: Over 100,000 hill residents uprooted; fertile terraces, family shrines, and cultural history drowned under 40 square kilometers of water.
Bahuguna's final epitaph: 'This is a dam built with our tears.'
Enduring lesson: Genuine development cannot be measured solely in megawatts and concrete; it must be measured by justice, safety, and respect for living communities.
slides.mental_model: A sunken ghost city beneath a scenic vacation lake: tourists see boat rides on blue water, but displaced families see the drowned ruins of their ancestral homes beneath the surface.

checkpoint.question: What was Sunderlal Bahuguna's mournful final verdict when the Tehri Dam reservoir swallowed Old Tehri town?
options: This is a dam built with our tears
A temple of modern India has risen
Technology has triumphed over nature
The Himalayan rivers are finally conquered
checkpoint.explanation: After fighting the project for decades and seeing his own shelter submerged by rising waters, Sunderlal Bahuguna famously wept: 'This is a dam built with our tears.'
